questions.topic: Why a metal wire's resistance rises when it is heated
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a metal wire's resistance increases when it is heated
questions.stem: A memo note asks why the tram overhead copper wire reads higher resistance in August afternoons than in winter mornings. Which reasoning does the memo's engineering appendix give?

options.text: Hotter metal conducts better because the heat speeds the electrons along the wire faster
options.misconception: treats heat as a driving force that speeds up electrons

options.text: Hotter metal conducts better because its atoms are further apart and so easier to push aside
options.misconception: links hotter metal with larger spacing instead of stronger scattering

options.text: Hotter metal has more vigorous lattice vibrations, so the moving electrons are scattered more often
Hotter metal conducts better because the wire expands and shortens the path the charge must take
options.misconception: explains the change through geometric shortening rather than scattering

questions.explanation: Metal ions vibrate more strongly as the temperature rises, and the resulting scattering of conduction electrons raises the resistance. Neither faster electrons nor a shorter wire would raise it, since both would lower it.

questions.topic: Why one cell drives different currents in different circuits

questions.stem: A maintenance note compares two substation feeders: one delivers a 1.5 A lamp circuit and the other a 6.0 A pump circuit, both taken from the same 24 V battery. Explain why those currents differ.

answer.exemplar: Each feeder presents a different total resistance to the battery, and the battery's own internal resistance sits in series with both, so the current each draws is set by that combined resistance rather than by the battery voltage alone. The lamp feeder has the higher resistance and therefore draws the smaller current, while the pump feeder's lower resistance draws more, even though both are supplied by the same cell.

questions.explanation: A cell drives whatever current the total circuit resistance allows, so a lamp feeder with a higher resistance draws less than a pump feeder with a lower one. The shared voltage does not force a shared current.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Resistance from material, length and cross-section
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the material of a conductor affects its resistance
questions.stem: A memo explains why the new feeder was specified in aluminium rather than copper, noting that both cables have the same length and cross-section. Explain the physics behind that choice.

answer.exemplar: Resistance depends on the material through its resistivity as well as on the length and the cross-section, so for identical geometry two metals can differ markedly. Aluminium has a higher resistivity than copper and would need a larger cross-section for the same loss, but it is far lighter, so over long spans the weight and cost of supporting a thicker copper conductor can outweigh the extra area that aluminium needs.

questions.explanation: Resistance is resistivity times length over cross-section, and resistivity belongs to the material. For identical geometry a different metal gives a different resistance, which is why the appendix compares materials too.
questions.hint: The material sets a factor of its own.

questions.topic: Resistance from material, length and cross-section
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a feeder cable is specified with a larger cross-section
questions.stem: A memo explains why the substation feeder specification calls for a larger cross-section than the old cable. Explain the reasoning behind that choice.

answer.exemplar: For a given material and length the resistance of a conductor falls in inverse proportion to its cross-sectional area, so doubling the area halves the resistance and cuts the voltage drop along the run for the same current. A larger section therefore means less power wasted as heat in the cable and a smaller voltage drop at the distant end, which is why the appendix asks for more copper even though it costs more and weighs more to support.

questions.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area for a fixed material and length, so a larger section lowers both the voltage drop along the run and the power wasted as heat in the cable.
questions.hint: Compare the area factor with the loss factor.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a metal wire's resistance rises when it is heated
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a wire's resistance at a temperature below the reference value
questions.stem: A tram contact wire has a resistance of 0.0100 ohms per metre, and the appendix notes that copper's resistance falls by 0.4 percent for each kelvin below 20 degrees Celsius. What resistance, in ohms, does a 300 m run have at 10 degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: At 20 degrees the 300 m run has a resistance of 0.0100 times 300, which is 3.000 ohms. A 10 kelvin drop is a 4 percent reduction, and 4 percent of 3.000 ohms is 0.120 ohms, leaving 2.88 ohms.
questions.hint: Find the 20 degree resistance, then apply the percentage drop.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Current density and the carriers that carry it
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the current density in a high-current conductor
questions.stem: A depot note records a current of 300 A in a conductor of cross-section 150 square millimetres. What current density, in amperes per square millimetre, does the appendix quote?
questions.explanation: Current density is the current divided by the cross-sectional area carrying it, so 300 A over 150 square millimetres gives 2 A per square millimetre. Engineers compare that figure with the conductor's permitted rating.
questions.hint: Divide the current by the cross-sectional area.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Energy stored in a charged capacitor
questions.learningObjective: Combine the energies of two capacitors charged to different voltages
questions.stem: A signal cabinet's capacitor of 1000 microfarad is charged to 24.0 V, and the appendix asks how much energy a second identical capacitor at 12.0 V adds. Which combined figure follows?

options.text: The first stores 0.288 J and the second 0.144 J, giving 0.432 J together
options.misconception: treats halving the voltage as leaving the energy unchanged

options.text: The first stores 0.288 J and the second 0.072 J, giving 0.360 J together
The first stores 0.144 J and the second 0.072 J, giving 0.216 J together
options.misconception: omits the factor of one half in the energy formula

options.text: The first stores 0.288 J and the second 0.072 J, giving 0.216 J together
options.misconception: adds the two figures incorrectly

questions.explanation: The first capacitor stores half of 0.001 farads times 24 squared, which is 0.288 J, and the second at half the voltage stores a quarter of that, 0.072 J. Together they hold 0.360 J.
questions.hint: Halving the voltage quarters the stored energy.
